title: PolarWindow
description: A CLPS lunar mission browser for exploring landing sites, sunlight windows, and Earth contact using public NASA terrain and mission data.
impact: Contributing research and data preparation for mission constraints, with frontend work planned next.
overview: PolarWindow is an independent lunar mission exploration project being developed for the NASA International Space Apps Challenge. It brings CLPS mission information, terrain-aware sunlight analysis, and Earth visibility into a visual planning interface. It is not a NASA product or an operational mission certification tool.
problem: A promising lunar landing site is not defined by coordinates alone. Local terrain can block sunlight or Earth visibility, and a single combined score can hide long periods of darkness or lost contact. Comparing candidate sites requires the underlying assumptions and data sources to remain visible.
solution: Organize mission and landing-site exploration around separate sunlight, Earth-contact, longest-darkness, and longest-no-contact measures. Connect map and skyline views to source-grounded calculations, while clearly labeling saved data, fallbacks, and uncertainty.
architecture: A React and Three.js interface consumes typed FastAPI endpoints. Python geometry and ephemeris calculations are separated from API and application services, with PostgreSQL persistence and background workers for computation and data feeds. NASA LOLA terrain and JPL/NAIF SPICE data support the analysis; a labeled snapshot mode allows browsing a saved copy without the full backend.

architectureDiagram.caption: From public lunar data to an explorable mission and landing-site view.

features.title: Mission and site exploration
features.description: Browse CLPS deliveries and compare candidate landing locations through linked visual views.

features.title: Separate visibility measures
features.description: Inspect illumination and Earth contact independently, including the longest interruptions rather than only total available hours.

features.title: Terrain-aware skylines
features.description: Explore how the local horizon changes Sun and Earth visibility over a selected date range.

features.title: Traceable planning outputs
features.description: Inspect data provenance, saved-copy labels, and exportable planning reports and intervals.

challenges.challenge: Communicating the limits of a planning model
challenges.learned: Expose source provenance and fallback assumptions alongside the visual result; illumination is not a thermal-survival or operational go/no-go guarantee.

challenges.challenge: Keeping exploration separate from expensive calculations
challenges.learned: Separate browser presentation, service orchestration, and pure geometry so computed results and saved snapshots have clear boundaries.

contribution: My work focuses on research and mission-analysis inputs: wind checks, finer terrain for rover line of sight, and launch-window constraints from launch-pad direction limits. Supporting work involves SPENVIS and Copernicus Marine data access and ESA Lunar Pathfinder orbit documentation. These analysis areas are ongoing; frontend implementation is my next planned contribution.

title: Complete Legal Aid
description: Bilingual legal-aid platform connecting Bangladeshi citizens with verified lawyers — escrow payments, encrypted evidence, and four AI agents on one real-time stack.
contribution: I worked on both the frontend and backend of Complete Legal Aid, connecting user-facing interfaces with application services and end-to-end workflows.
impact: Produced a deployable justice platform rather than a demo: Docker Compose brings up PostgreSQL, Redis, Daphne, nginx, and certbot with automatic TLS, and production settings actively refuse to start with DEBUG on, SQLite, or default passwords.
overview: Legal help in Bangladesh is hard to price, hard to verify, and hard to reach. CLA puts citizens, verified lawyers, and administrators on one platform in both Bangla and English, and treats the awkward parts of the problem — proving a lawyer is real, holding money safely until work is done, and keeping evidence private — as first-class features rather than afterthoughts.
problem: A citizen looking for legal help has no reliable way to check that a lawyer is genuine, no protection when paying up front, and no safe channel for sensitive documents. Lawyers, meanwhile, lose hours drafting standard filings by hand. Both sides fall back on personal referrals, which excludes anyone without the right contacts.
solution: Every role gets its own dashboard over a shared Django backend. Payments run through an escrow flow with an immutable ledger, so money is only released against completed work and the books can be proven consistent. Evidence never sits at a public URL — nginx denies /media by default and files are reachable only through short-lived signed links. Four server-side AI agents handle triage, case-strength estimation, drafting, and emergency routing, each restricted to an allow-listed set of tools and scoped to the caller's role.
architecture: The stack is event-driven rather than poll-driven: a service or signal pushes through a Redis channel layer into Django Channels, and the browser's WebSocket provider updates the UI directly. Polling exists only as a fallback. The AI layer is deliberately isolated — all keys stay server-side, and every AI feature degrades gracefully to a non-AI path when a key or an optional ML dependency is missing, so a missing API key never takes the platform down.

architectureDiagram.caption: Complete Legal Aid pushes state changes outward through Redis and Django Channels; the browser subscribes rather than polls.

features.title: Four scoped AI agents
features.description: Counsel Match triages a citizen's problem into a ranked lawyer shortlist; Justice Lens gives a calibrated case-strength estimate with cited articles; Document Forge drafts from a lawyer's own cases and flags unfilled placeholders; Sentinel handles emergency triage with anonymity-respecting NGO routing. All use function-calling against allow-listed tools, stream over SSE, and are throttled per user.

features.title: Escrow payments on an immutable ledger
features.description: SSLCommerz payments flow through a single audited path that writes append-only WalletLedgerEntry records. A reconcile_wallets management command proves the ledger and balances agree.

features.title: Signed-link evidence vault
features.description: Evidence, identity papers, and chat attachments are never served from public URLs. nginx default-denies /media except explicit public folders; everything else is reachable only via short-lived signed links, behind extension, MIME, and magic-byte validation with a 25 MB cap.

features.title: Constitution RAG in plain Bangla
features.description: A Gemini-backed assistant answers in everyday Bangla, retrieving over the Constitution with FAISS so answers cite real articles instead of paraphrasing from memory.

features.title: Ban-aware JWT sessions
features.description: One-hour access tokens with seven-day rotating refresh and a blacklist. Banning a user invalidates their existing tokens immediately rather than waiting for expiry.

features.title: Court-ready bilingual drafting
features.description: Generates bail applications, deeds, notices, and affidavits in Bangla or English from lawyer-owned, database-backed templates that can be shared across the firm.

challenges.challenge: Keeping money movement auditable when payments, refunds, and withdrawals all touch the same balance.
challenges.learned: Routed every balance change through one service instead of letting views update wallets directly, and made the ledger append-only so a mistake produces a correcting entry rather than a silent edit. That made a reconciliation command possible — consistency became something to verify on demand rather than assume.

challenges.challenge: Confidential uploads are easy to leak, because the obvious setup serves them from a guessable static path.
challenges.learned: Inverted the default: nginx denies everything under /media unless explicitly allowed, and private files are reachable only through expiring signed links. Deny-by-default means a new upload type is private until someone deliberately publishes it — the opposite of the usual failure mode.

challenges.challenge: The on-box ML extras (FAISS, sentence-transformers) pull in torch at roughly 2.5 GB, which is unacceptable in a CI image.
challenges.learned: Split them into a separate requirements-ml.txt and made every dependent feature detect their absence and fall back. The Docker image and CI skip them entirely, and the same codebase runs in both shapes without branching.

challenges.challenge: Giving LLM agents real capability without giving them free rein over the database.
challenges.learned: Each agent gets an explicit allow-list of tools and inherits the caller's role, so a citizen's agent cannot reach a lawyer's cases. Capability is granted per tool rather than withheld per query, which is far easier to reason about when reviewing what an agent can actually do.

results.description: Counsel Match, Justice Lens, Document Forge, Sentinel — each role-scoped and tool-restricted
Citizen, lawyer, and admin, each with a separate code-split dashboard
Full i18n with Bangla code-split from the main bundle
PostgreSQL 16, Redis 7, Daphne, nginx, and certbot via one Docker Compose deploy

title: Dawat
description: A Bangla-first wedding invitation platform in development: publish a Jamdani-inspired card, give each household a personal link, and track replies for the events they are actually invited to.
impact: Built the invitation-to-response workflow around named households, versioned publishing, private photos, and separate seller and couple workspaces; launch qualification is ongoing.
overview: Dawat turns a Bengali wedding invitation into a managed guest workflow. A couple edits a Bangla-first, Jamdani-inspired invitation, publishes a version, and shares personal household links. Guests see the events selected for their household and can reply or leave a wish without creating an account. A general invitation link remains view-only. The repository contains working seller, couple, and guest flows, but the project is still in development: physical-phone performance, operational recovery, and commercial handoff remain open work.
problem: A beautiful digital card does not solve the host's planning problem. One family may be invited to the wedding only, another to both ceremonies; a reply from a household must carry a headcount rather than merely a name. Meanwhile, invitation details and photos change during preparation. Sharing an editable draft risks exposing unfinished content, while collecting replies through a general public form makes it difficult to know which household answered and which events they were allowed to attend.
solution: Separate editing, publication, and guest access. The couple saves a private draft and explicitly publishes a version before sharing. Each named household receives an event allowance and a personal link; guests do not type an arbitrary identity into a public RSVP form. The host dashboard collects attendance, headcounts, and wishes, supports attributed corrections, and exports a private CSV for planning. Seller confirmation and customer activation are separate steps, so placing an order alone does not grant a management workspace.
architecture: Next.js App Router serves the Bangla/English workspaces, invitation pages, and server API routes. Supabase Auth supplies verified customer sessions, while PostgreSQL row-level policies and narrow transaction functions enforce wedding membership and permitted mutations. Draft revisions detect stale saves; publishing creates an immutable version rather than exposing the live editor. Guest access uses random link tokens with stored digests and wedding/household-bound AES-GCM encryption for recoverable host copying. Photos pass through a bounded Sharp processor into a private Storage bucket; application routes recheck publication or guest access before serving a referenced variant.

architectureDiagram.caption: Private preparation becomes a published invitation; named household access controls replies and photo delivery.

layers.edgeLabel: Transactional commands and protected media reads

nodes.detail: Customer sessions and seller MFA gate

features.title: Invite a family to the right ceremonies
features.description: Create a named household, assign one or both events, and share its personal link. Attendance and headcount stay attached to that household and event scope. A general invitation can be forwarded for viewing without opening an anonymous RSVP form.

features.title: Edit privately, then publish deliberately
features.description: Change names, venue details, or photos in a draft without immediately changing the guest-facing invitation. Revision checks reject stale saves, and explicit publication creates a retained version. The workspace distinguishes unsaved, saved, and published state instead of treating a successful keystroke as a public update.

features.title: Turn replies into a working guest list
features.description: Review attendance and wishes in the couple workspace, make an attributed correction when a family updates its plans, and export a private CSV. This supports the concrete task of reconciling household responses for event planning rather than presenting only a decorative response counter.

features.title: Keep couple photos behind the invitation gate
features.description: Accept up to five active photos, decode and validate the uploaded image, strip embedded location metadata, and create 480/960/1600 WebP variants without upscaling. Drafts stay private; guest photo reads recheck current access. Revoking a household link blocks future scoped reads, though previously downloaded copies cannot be recalled.

features.title: Hand the correct workspace to the customer
features.description: The seller confirms an order and separately activates the intended verified customer. Database transactions check the wedding, current grant, and entitlement, while seller actions require a staff identity and MFA. This addresses accidental access to another couple's preparation workspace at the data boundary as well as in navigation.

challenges.challenge: A guest link is an access credential, not just a share URL
challenges.learned: The code separates token digests used for lookup from encrypted copies used by the host's copy action, binds encryption to the wedding and household, and provides rotation and revocation. The practical tradeoff is that access can be stopped for future requests, but content already saved by a guest cannot be withdrawn.

challenges.challenge: Invitation edits must not silently change a household's event scope
challenges.learned: A dedicated migration preserves household event assignments rather than expanding them when invitation configuration changes. Publication state, event selection, and named-link permissions must agree; a newly enabled ceremony is not automatically permission to invite every existing household.

challenges.challenge: Retries and stale tabs can corrupt otherwise simple forms
challenges.learned: Draft revisions surface concurrent edits, while command replay and row locks protect transactional mutations. Photo reservation and upload are separate, bounded steps so retrying a slow upload does not silently allocate another slot. Recovery state is part of the workflow, not just an error toast.

challenges.challenge: Implementation evidence is not launch evidence
challenges.learned: The repository includes integration tests for database isolation, guest delivery, media processing, and workspace behavior. Its release notes still leave phone performance, recovery operations, and commercial delivery open; the portfolio therefore presents Dawat as ongoing and makes no adoption, revenue, or production-readiness claim.

title: Duet
description: A couples app in development, bringing one-to-one messaging, shared memories, date planning, and daily connection rituals into one personal space.
impact: A couples app in development, bringing one-to-one messaging, shared memories, date planning, and daily connection rituals into one personal space.
overview: Duet is a mobile app in development for two people to share everyday moments. It combines messaging, memories, date ideas, and small daily rituals with a warm visual system and an offline local mode.
problem: Conversations, photos, plans, and little relationship rituals are often scattered across unrelated apps. A dedicated shared space needs to feel personal while keeping pairing, local state, and optional synchronization understandable.
solution: Bring the core experiences into a coordinated mobile interface: a conversation, a shared memory timeline, date planning, and daily prompts. Keep local usage available and support optional Firebase synchronization for a paired experience.
architecture: React Native and Expo power the mobile interface, navigation, and device integrations. TypeScript models and shared UI primitives connect the feature screens to local persistence and optional Firebase services. Suggestions use an interchangeable provider interface; the current offline implementation selects curated text by context and tone, rather than running an on-device language model.

features.title: A shared conversation
features.description: Messaging screens support text, photos, voice notes, reactions, and stickers in a one-to-one experience.

features.title: Memories and small rituals
features.description: Collect shared moments and use daily questions with mutual reveal to encourage regular connection.

features.title: Date planning and suggestions
features.description: Plan time together and explore tone-based message drafts and occasion-based gift ideas through the offline suggestion provider.

features.title: Device-aware privacy controls
features.description: App-lock and local-vault flows use Expo device capabilities and are being developed alongside pairing and synchronization.

challenges.challenge: Designing a cohesive experience across many small features
challenges.learned: Use shared typography, spacing, motion, and component primitives so messaging, memories, and rituals feel like parts of the same app.

challenges.challenge: Supporting local use alongside optional cloud services
challenges.learned: Keep persistence and suggestion providers behind explicit interfaces so the app can evolve without tying every screen to a remote service.

contribution: I am building Duet independently across the React Native interface, application state, local storage, optional Firebase integration, and suggestion-provider architecture. The app is still in development.

title: RadFlow
description: Offline-first AI radiology triage platform for district hospitals — dual CV/VLM pipelines turn a chest X-ray into a guideline-grounded report on CPU, GPU, or Apple Silicon alike.
contribution: I worked on RadFlow’s frontend and UI/UX: designing and implementing the interface for the team’s radiology triage prototype. The AI models, inference pipelines, and backend architecture described here are team-level system features, not claims of my individual implementation.
impact: Built the FastAPI backend that turns a hackathon model demo into an operable system: a retrying async inference queue, a per-endpoint latency/error observability panel, and a 7-day confidence-drift report comparing recent cases against baseline — the parts a research pipeline needs before anyone would trust it on a ward.
overview: Built at the Harvard Health Systems Innovation Lab Hackathon 2026 by a four-person team, RadFlow targets a specific gap: district and rural hospitals that own an X-ray machine but have no radiologist on site. It runs two complete AI pipelines end to end — detection, localization, guideline retrieval, and report drafting — entirely offline, and auto-adapts to whatever hardware the hospital actually has.
problem: A district hospital can own imaging hardware without owning imaging expertise — the read is the bottleneck, not the scan. Cloud-based triage tools assume reliable connectivity and a specific GPU, neither of which holds in a resource-constrained facility, and a missed abnormality on a chest film has a direct clinical cost.
solution: Every radiograph moves through a 4-stage pipeline — DenseNet121 screens for 18 pathologies, GradCAM localizes and crops the abnormal region, a ChromaDB-backed RAG step retrieves the matching clinical guideline, and CheXagent-8b drafts the final report grounded in that guideline rather than free-associating. A second pipeline, the Foveal Engine, trades some of that depth for speed: an OpenCV contrast pass crops a high-resolution region of interest in milliseconds and a token router (D-RoVA) drops irrelevant visual tokens before the VLM ever sees them, cutting token count by roughly 80% while keeping the crop diagnostic.
architecture: A FastAPI backend fronts both pipelines behind one API and owns the parts that make it operable rather than a demo: an InferenceJob queue processed by a background worker thread with retries, per-job cancellation, and status polling, so a slow VLM call never blocks the request path. Every completed inference is written to an append-only InferenceLedger, which powers an admin drift report comparing the last 7 days of case mix and calibrated confidence against the 7 days before — the kind of check a clinical tool needs and a hackathon demo usually skips. A hardware router picks CUDA + bitsandbytes 4-bit quantization, Apple MLX, or Intel IPEX at startup, so the same code path runs on whatever machine is actually in the building.

architectureDiagram.caption: A radiograph moves through detection, localization, guideline retrieval, and VLM drafting — queued, retried, and logged for drift review rather than returned as a single blocking call.

features.title: RadFlow-Edge: 4-stage clinical pipeline
features.description: DenseNet121 detection over 18 pathologies, GradCAM localization and cropping, ChromaDB-backed guideline retrieval, and a CheXagent-8b VLM analyzer that drafts the final report grounded in the retrieved guideline.

features.title: Foveal Engine: sub-second triage path
features.description: An OpenCV 'Vision Hack' crops a 512x512 region of interest by contrast alone, and a D-RoVA token router drops irrelevant visual tokens before the VLM call — roughly an 80% token reduction with the crop still diagnostic.

features.title: Async inference queue with retry and cancel
features.description: Analysis requests enqueue as an InferenceJob worked by a background thread with up to 2 retries and a live status/progress endpoint, so a slow or failed VLM call degrades gracefully instead of timing out the request.

features.title: Observability and drift panels
features.description: Per-endpoint call count, average and p95 latency, and error rate are tracked in-process; a separate drift report compares the last 7 days of pathology mix and calibrated confidence against the prior 7-day baseline.

features.title: Hardware-agile inference
features.description: Auto-detects NVIDIA CUDA (with 4-bit bitsandbytes quantization), Apple Silicon (MLX/MPS), or Intel ARC (IPEX) at startup so the identical pipeline runs on a hospital's existing hardware without a rebuild.

features.title: Dynamic clinical worklist
features.description: A full case worklist with escalation events and an EHR-style timeline per patient, backed by SQLAlchemy models (Case, Finding, Escalation) rather than being bolted onto the inference response.

challenges.challenge: A VLM call (CheXagent-8b) can legitimately take long enough to make a synchronous request path feel broken, and a hackathon demo can't afford a hung request.
challenges.learned: Moved inference behind a queue: a POST returns a job ID immediately, a worker thread processes it with retries, and the frontend polls status. Cancellation and a hard retry cap made the failure modes explicit instead of a request that just never returns.

challenges.challenge: Reducing visual tokens by 80% (the Foveal Engine's core bet) is only useful if the crop that remains is still the diagnostically relevant one.
challenges.learned: Kept the contrast-based crop (Vision Hack) as a distinct, inspectable stage before any token-dropping, so the tradeoff between speed and detail is a visible pipeline boundary rather than a black box the VLM has to compensate for.

challenges.challenge: A model that quietly degrades — starts favoring different pathologies, or grows less confident — is worse than one that fails loudly, and nothing in a single-request API surfaces that.
challenges.learned: Added the drift endpoint specifically to compare rolling windows against each other from data already being logged, so the question 'has this gotten worse' has an answer without exporting the database somewhere else first.

title: AI Orchestrator (OrchestratorCLI)
description: Desktop app that routes coding tasks to whichever AI CLI — Claude Code, Gemini, Copilot, Codex, Cline — is actually available, with automatic failover before any of them hits a rate limit.
contribution: I contributed to the frontend as well as Windows runtime and packaging support. This is a collaborative project led by Md Ahbab; the overall orchestration architecture and all platform features should not be attributed to me alone.
impact: Fixed the bug that crashed every terminal spawned by the Windows-packaged build (pywinpty needs a null-terminated environment-block string, not a list), added a 10-second spawn timeout so a stuck PTY fails loudly instead of hanging the UI, and extended the desktop build pipeline to bundle backend Python dependencies into the installer.
overview: A desktop Electron app, led by teammate Md Ahbab, that treats every AI coding CLI a developer might have installed — Claude Code, Gemini, Copilot, Codex, Cline, and others — as an interchangeable backend behind one orchestrator. A central planner (Grok, Gemini, or DeepSeek, in that fallback order) plans and dispatches work across them in parallel, over real PTY-backed terminal sessions rather than screen-scraped output.
problem: Juggling several AI coding CLIs by hand means manually noticing when one hits a rate limit, re-typing context into whichever tool is free, and getting no parallelism even when a task splits cleanly across agents. Packaging that as a desktop app adds its own failure class: process spawning, credential storage, and terminal I/O all behave differently on Windows than on the POSIX systems most CLI tooling is written for.
solution: The orchestrator plans a task, splits it into divisions, and dispatches each division to a CLI agent through a PTY session it owns end to end — spawn, resize, kill, and process-tree teardown all go through one service. Providers are health-sorted (online before limited before offline) so failover is visible in the UI, not just silent. A user-defined CLI registry lets someone register a coding agent the app doesn't know about out of the box, validated the same way the built-in ones are.
architecture: Electron wraps a React/TypeScript frontend and a local FastAPI + SQLite backend, so the desktop build and the browser dev build share the same code paths. Real-time terminal I/O and orchestrator events stream over WebSocket; REST covers sessions, providers, and settings. On Windows specifically, PTY spawning goes through pywinpty's low-level API, which — unlike the POSIX path — expects the process environment as a single null-terminated block string rather than a list of key/value pairs.

architectureDiagram.caption: A central planner dispatches divisions of one task to parallel CLI agents, each running in a real PTY session the backend owns end to end.

features.title: Multi-provider planning with automatic failover
features.description: A central planner (Grok, falling back to Gemini, then DeepSeek) breaks a task into divisions and routes each to a coding CLI agent, retrying against the next healthy provider rather than surfacing a rate-limit error to the user.

features.title: Real PTY-backed terminal sessions
features.description: Each dispatched agent runs in an actual pseudo-terminal the orchestrator manages — spawn, resize, and kill all go through one PtySession service, with process-tree teardown (taskkill /T on Windows, process groups on POSIX) so a killed session doesn't leave orphans.

features.title: Custom CLI registry
features.description: Users can register their own coding CLI (slug, command template, verb map) through a Settings tab; custom entries are validated and merged into the same registry the built-in agents use.

features.title: Health-sorted provider display
features.description: Providers are ordered online > limited > offline (then by name) everywhere they're listed — the providers panel, the collapsed sidebar, and onboarding — so which agent is actually usable right now is visible at a glance.

features.title: Encrypted local credential storage
features.description: API keys for each provider are encrypted at rest, with production configuration required to fail fast rather than silently mint a throwaway encryption key that would brick stored credentials later.

features.title: Cross-platform desktop packaging
features.description: electron-builder produces signed Windows, macOS, and Linux installers with the FastAPI backend bundled via extraResources rather than PyInstaller, plus an auto-updater wired through IPC.

challenges.challenge: Every terminal spawned by the Windows-packaged build crashed, because pywinpty's low-level spawn call expected the process environment as a single null-terminated block string, not the list of "KEY=VALUE" strings the POSIX path uses.
challenges.learned: Rebuilt the Windows branch to join the environment into a `\0`-joined block with a trailing terminator, guarding against embedded nulls in any key or value. The fix only surfaces on an actual packaged Windows build, not in dev, which is exactly the kind of platform gap that's invisible until someone runs the installer.

challenges.challenge: A PTY spawn could hang indefinitely on Windows with no timeout, leaving a runtime stuck in a 'starting' state that the UI had no way to recover from.
challenges.learned: Wrapped the spawn call in `asyncio.wait_for` with a 10-second budget, and on timeout explicitly marked the runtime row 'failed' in the database instead of leaving it in limbo — a hang and a crash need different handling, and only one of them was covered before.

challenges.challenge: The session-creation path had a double-checked-locking bug: the existence check ran inside one lock scope but the session got constructed and inserted outside it, so two near-simultaneous requests for the same runtime could each build a full PTY session before either was registered.
challenges.learned: Moved session construction inside the same lock as the existence check, and added an explicit kill-and-replace path for the loser instead of leaking an unregistered process. Narrowing the lock window is only safe once every write it's supposed to protect is actually inside it.

results.description: Claude Code, Gemini, Copilot, Codex, Cline, and other registered CLIs, dispatched in parallel
Grok, then Gemini, then DeepSeek — automatic on rate limit or failure
Electron installers built via electron-builder with a bundled Python backend
Hard budget added to PTY spawn so a stuck Windows terminal fails visibly

title: SkillEx
description: Peer skill-exchange platform where people trade what they can teach for what they want to learn — matched semantically, with no money involved.
impact: The OOP brief pushed toward structure that earned its keep: one client boundary on the frontend and an interface-per-service split on the backend meant the embedding provider could be swapped for a local fallback without touching a controller.
overview: An Advanced OOP course project taken past the coursework brief. The interesting constraint is that there is no currency: a match is only useful when two people's offers and wants genuinely complement each other, which turns matching into the core engineering problem rather than a feature bolted on later.
problem: Skill learning is gated by cost, while plenty of people hold knowledge worth trading. Keyword matching is not good enough to pair them — someone offering "React" and someone wanting "frontend development" never meet, even though they should.
solution: Skills are embedded through the Gemini Embedding API and matched by semantic similarity, so related phrasings converge. Because a hosted embedding service is a hard dependency for a course project, the backend falls back to local embeddings whenever no API key is present — the feature degrades in quality rather than disappearing.
architecture: A monorepo with clean seams. The frontend is organised as feature-first vertical slices, and all network access funnels through a single ApiClient singleton, so JWT attachment and error shape live in one place. The backend keeps controllers thin and routes work through service interfaces to implementations, with Flyway owning the schema as versioned SQL.

architectureDiagram.caption: SkillEx request path: a React feature slice calls through a single API client into a layered Spring Boot backend.

layers.title: Client - React 19 + Vite
layers.edgeLabel: HTTP JSON, proxied by Vite in dev

features.title: Semantic skill matching
features.description: Gemini embeddings place offered and wanted skills in the same vector space, so "React" and "frontend development" match on meaning rather than on shared characters.

features.title: Graceful embedding fallback
features.description: With EMBEDDING_PROVIDER set to api but no key present, the backend silently switches to local embeddings instead of failing the request.

features.title: Single API boundary
features.description: An ApiClient singleton wraps fetch, attaches the JWT, and normalises every response into ApiResponse<T> — so success, error, and message handling are identical across features.

features.title: Versioned schema with Flyway
features.description: Migrations run as ordered SQL on startup, so a fresh clone reaches the current schema without anyone running statements by hand.

features.title: Feature-first frontend slices
features.description: Each domain owns its components, services, and types together, so a feature can be read or removed without tracing through shared folders.

challenges.challenge: A hosted embedding API is a single point of failure for the one feature the product is built around.
challenges.learned: Made the provider a configuration choice with an automatic local fallback rather than a hard dependency. Designing the degraded path first meant the feature had a defined behaviour without a key, instead of an exception.

challenges.challenge: Getting a Spring Boot backend and a Vite frontend running together locally involves MySQL, ports, and migration order.
challenges.learned: Automated it — a pre-start script detects and starts MySQL, waits for port 3306, and ensures the database exists before the backend boots. Setup friction is a real cost on a team project; removing it is worth the scripting.

challenges.challenge: Thin controllers are easy to describe and easy to erode once deadlines arrive.
challenges.learned: Keeping the service as an interface with a separate implementation made the boundary structural rather than a convention. It is harder to leak business logic into a controller when doing so means bypassing a type you would have to go around deliberately.

results.description: Gemini embeddings, with an automatic local fallback
React 19 frontend and Spring Boot 3 backend sharing one migration source
Versioned SQL applied automatically on first run

title: ConvoVerse
description: HCI research prototype where introverted learners rehearse conversations with LLM agents before facing the real thing.
impact: Contributes a reusable interaction pattern rather than a product: staged exposure, reversible actions, and non-evaluative feedback, applicable to any system supporting participation.
overview: An academic Human-Computer Interaction project built on a specific claim: many capable students stay quiet not from lack of knowledge but from lack of rehearsal. ConvoVerse gives them a private space to practise, positioning AI as a facilitator that helps someone feel ready to participate — explicitly not as a substitute for talking to people.
problem: Educational platforms optimise for delivering content and assume participation follows. For students who freeze in discussions, the barrier is social readiness, and every existing option asks them to practise in exactly the public setting they are avoiding.
solution: Difficulty is scaffolded in stages instead of thrown at the user. Observer Mode lets them watch agents converse without participating; then one-on-one with a single peer agent; then a small group where a Peer, a Group Member, and a Facilitator compete for turns. Rewind and Retry lets any exchange be restarted with no penalty.
architecture: The same agent roles are recombined per stage rather than rewritten, so escalating difficulty is a matter of how many agents are present and how they interact. Psychological safety is enforced as a design constraint: no scoring, no public exposure, no forced turn — closing feedback is reflective rather than evaluative.

architectureDiagram.caption: ConvoVerse raises social difficulty in stages, each backed by a different arrangement of the same LLM agents.

features.title: Observer Mode
features.description: The user watches AI agents hold a conversation with no expectation of input, so the first exposure carries no risk of being addressed.

features.title: Three distinct agent roles
features.description: A Peer converses as an equal, a Group Member competes for speaking turns, and a Facilitator keeps discussion moving — together modelling the dynamics that make group settings hard.

features.title: Rewind and Retry
features.description: Any exchange can be restarted to try a different response, making exploration free and removing the cost of saying the wrong thing.

features.title: Adaptive pacing
features.description: Conversation speed and complexity respond to the user's comfort rather than following a fixed script.

features.title: Non-evaluative reflection
features.description: Sessions close with reflective prompts rather than a score, keeping the experience about confidence instead of performance.

challenges.challenge: An AI conversation partner risks becoming a substitute for human contact — the opposite of the intended outcome.
challenges.learned: Framed every interaction as rehearsal for a real conversation rather than a replacement, and made the staging always point outward toward participation. The framing is the intervention here; the same agents with different framing would produce a different, worse product.

challenges.challenge: Scoring is the obvious way to show progress, and exactly the wrong mechanic for anxious users.
challenges.learned: Dropped scores entirely in favour of reflective prompts. Any evaluative signal reintroduces the judgement the environment exists to remove, so the safety property has to be enforced by leaving features out.

results.description: Peer, Group Member, and Facilitator, recombined per stage
Observe, one-on-one, then small group
Reflective feedback only — a deliberate design constraint

title: Care Companion
description: Raspberry Pi health rover that monitors vitals, dispenses medication on schedule, and raises alerts for gas, fire, or a panic button.
impact: Built entirely from commodity parts — Pi 4, Arduino UNO, DHT11, MQ-2, a pulse sensor, an L298N driver — keeping the whole prototype within a student budget while covering monitoring, reminders, hazard detection, and mobility.
overview: A microprocessor project that ended up a working prototype: a mobile assistant for patients and elderly people living at home, combining continuous vitals monitoring with physical actions — moving to the patient, opening a medicine drawer, sounding an alarm.
problem: Home care depends on someone being present. Missed medication, an unnoticed fever, a gas leak, or a fall can all go undetected for hours, and commercial monitoring systems are priced out of reach for most households.
solution: Split the work across two processors by what each is good at. An Arduino UNO owns the sensors, where tight timing loops matter; the Raspberry Pi 4 handles vision, voice, decisions, and the web layer. They talk over serial, so a slow decision on the Pi never delays a sensor read.
architecture: The dashboard never talks to hardware. Sensor readings land in MySQL and the UI reads from there, with Django Channels pushing updates over WebSocket. Celery and Redis own scheduled medication reminders, so timing survives a page being closed — the browser is a view onto state, not a participant in control.

architectureDiagram.caption: Care Companion separates real-time sensing on the microcontroller from decision-making on the Pi, with the dashboard reading only from the database.

features.title: Continuous vitals monitoring
features.description: DHT11 for temperature and a Pulse Sensor Amped for heart rate, sampled on the Arduino and streamed to the Pi over serial for threshold checks.

features.title: Automated medication dispensing
features.description: An SG90 servo opens the correct drawer on schedule with a buzzer prompt, driven by Celery so the timing holds independently of the dashboard.

features.title: Hazard detection
features.description: MQ-2 gas and IR flame sensors raise immediate local alarms and push a notification to caregivers, without waiting on a network round trip.

features.title: Autonomous mobility
features.description: TT gear motors through an L298N driver, with Pi Camera v3 person detection and obstacle avoidance so the rover can reach the patient.

features.title: Voice control
features.description: Wake-word commands let a patient summon or direct the rover without reaching a screen or a button.

features.title: Caregiver dashboard
features.description: Live vitals and trend charts over WebSocket, plus a panic-button feed, reading from the database rather than polling hardware.

challenges.challenge: Sensor sampling and computer vision on one processor make each other unreliable — vision work starves the timing-sensitive reads.
challenges.learned: Gave the Arduino sole ownership of sensors and left the Pi to decisions and vision, with serial between them. Splitting by timing requirement rather than by feature is what made both halves predictable.

challenges.challenge: Medication reminders cannot depend on a browser being open, but the obvious implementation puts the timer in the request cycle.
challenges.learned: Moved scheduling into Celery with Redis as the broker, so reminders fire from a worker regardless of who is watching. Anything with real-world consequences belongs outside the request cycle.

challenges.challenge: Emergency alerts that travel through the web stack inherit its latency, which is the wrong trade for a gas leak.
challenges.learned: Made hazards trigger the local buzzer and LEDs directly on the device, then notify over the network as a second step. The safety-critical path should not depend on anything that can be slow or offline.

results.description: Temperature, pulse, gas, and flame, sampled continuously
Arduino UNO for sensing, Raspberry Pi 4 for decisions and vision
Hazards sound on-device before any network call

title: UniShare
description: Real-time campus marketplace and community app — listings, groups, and chat that update live over a single WebSocket connection.
impact: Shipped with a real test setup — Vitest plus React Testing Library — and GitHub Actions deploying the UI, which is the part most student projects skip.
overview: A university community platform where students list items, form groups, and message each other. The design constraint was that everything social should feel immediate: a new message or listing appears without a refresh, and without the app polling in the background.
problem: Campus buying, selling, and group coordination scatter across Facebook groups and messenger threads, where posts are unsearchable and nothing is scoped to the university. Rebuilding that on request-response alone would mean constant polling to feel current.
solution: One Socket.IO connection per client carries chat, notifications, and listing updates, with REST handling ordinary reads and writes. TanStack Query owns the cache, so a socket event invalidates the affected query rather than the UI hand-patching its own state.
architecture: Better-SQLite3 backs the server — synchronous and embedded, which removes connection-pool handling and async plumbing at this scale. Zod validates payloads at runtime on the client, so data crossing the socket boundary is checked rather than trusted to match its TypeScript type.

architectureDiagram.caption: UniShare holds one Socket.IO connection per client, so listings, chat, and notifications all update without polling.

layers.title: Client - React 19 + Vite
layers.edgeLabel: REST for reads, WebSocket for live updates

features.title: Live chat and notifications
features.description: Socket.IO carries messages and notifications over one duplex connection, with rooms scoping broadcasts to the people who should receive them.

features.title: Cache-driven UI updates
features.description: Socket events invalidate TanStack Query keys instead of mutating component state, so the refetch path is the same whether an update arrived by socket or by navigation.

features.title: Runtime-validated payloads
features.description: Zod schemas check incoming data at the boundary, catching shape mismatches that TypeScript types cannot enforce at runtime.

features.title: Tested and continuously deployed
features.description: Vitest with React Testing Library and JSDOM cover the UI, and GitHub Actions handles deployment.

challenges.challenge: Live updates and a client cache disagree easily — the socket says one thing while the cache still holds another.
challenges.learned: Stopped treating socket payloads as state and treated them as invalidation signals instead. Letting the query layer refetch keeps one source of truth; patching the cache directly from an event is where the two views drift apart.

challenges.challenge: Choosing a database for a project that must be trivial to run locally but still relational.
challenges.learned: Better-SQLite3 is synchronous and embedded, so there is no pool, no daemon, and no await on every query. At campus scale the simplicity is worth more than the concurrency a server-based database would add.

results.description: Chat, notifications, and listing updates share one connection
TypeScript throughout, with route-level code splitting
Vitest suite plus GitHub Actions deployment

title: ChefMate
description: Recipe finder that takes whatever is actually in your kitchen, in plain English, and ranks real recipes by how much of each one you can already make.
impact: Turned a text-matching problem into a retrieval one. Every result carries an explicit match score plus the matched and missing ingredient lists, so the ranking is legible instead of being a number the user has to trust.
overview: Most recipe sites work backwards: pick a dish, then go shopping. ChefMate starts from the ingredients already on hand and finds the closest matches, showing what is missing for each so the trade-off is visible before committing to a dish.
problem: Free-text ingredient input breaks naive matching immediately. "Tomatoes", "tomato", and a typo like "tomatos" are three different strings, and regional names diverge further — aubergine and eggplant are the same vegetable. Exact matching fragments the search space and returns nothing useful.
solution: A normalisation stage runs before any matching. spaCy lemmatises each token to its base form, a hand-curated synonym map reconciles regional names, and rapidfuzz corrects remaining typos against the known ingredient vocabulary at an 80% similarity threshold. Only the cleaned tokens reach the retrieval step, so the model never sees the raw mess.
architecture: Cuisine, diet, and meal-type filters are applied to the dataframe first, which shrinks the candidate set before any vectorisation happens. The surviving recipes are transformed by a fitted TF-IDF vectoriser and queried with k-nearest-neighbours; the model, vectoriser, and dataframe are pickled together so a request only pays for lookup, not training.

architectureDiagram.caption: ChefMate normalises free text before retrieval, and filters the candidate set before vectorising it.

features.title: Lemmatisation and synonym mapping
features.description: spaCy's en_core_web_sm reduces each ingredient to its lemma, then a curated map folds regional variants together — courgette to zucchini, garbanzo bean to chickpea, scallion to green onion.

features.title: Fuzzy correction against known vocabulary
features.description: rapidfuzz matches a mistyped ingredient to the closest term actually present in the dataset, accepting it only above an 80% similarity score so wrong corrections are rejected rather than guessed.

features.title: Filter-then-retrieve ordering
features.description: Cuisine, diet, and meal-type filters narrow the dataframe before vectorisation, so kNN searches a small relevant set instead of the whole corpus.

features.title: Transparent match scoring
features.description: Each result reports matched ingredients, missing ingredients, and a percentage computed from their overlap, so a low-ranked recipe explains itself.

challenges.challenge: The same ingredient arrives under many spellings, and exact matching treats each as unrelated.
challenges.learned: Normalisation had to be a distinct pipeline stage rather than a helper sprinkled through the matching code. Once every input passed through one funnel — lemma, then synonym, then fuzzy — the retrieval logic got simpler because it could assume clean tokens.

challenges.challenge: Fitting the vectoriser per request made responses slow enough to feel broken.
challenges.learned: Pickled the trained model, the fitted vectoriser, and the recipe dataframe as one artefact loaded at predict time. Keeping them together matters more than it looks: a vectoriser separated from the data it was fitted on produces silently wrong vectors.

results.description: Lemmatisation, synonym mapping, and fuzzy correction before any matching
Similarity floor below which a correction is rejected rather than guessed
Every recipe shows both lists alongside its overlap score

title: Integrated Healthcare Management System
description: Hospital management system covering appointments, prescriptions, ambulance dispatch, and a blood-donor registry across patient, doctor, and admin roles.
impact: Writing it without a framework meant confronting the problems frameworks normally hide: session fixation, output escaping, and role checks that must not be bypassable by navigating straight to a URL. Migration and demo-seed scripts keep the schema reproducible.
overview: Built on plain PHP and MySQL with no framework, which made every piece of plumbing — routing, sessions, access control, escaping — an explicit decision rather than something inherited. It covers the workflows a small hospital actually runs on, including the ones usually left out of student projects: ambulance booking and a blood bank.
problem: Small clinics run on paper and phone calls. Appointments, prescriptions, ambulance requests, and blood-donor contacts each live in a different notebook, so nobody can answer a simple question like which donors match a patient's blood group right now.
solution: One database behind role-separated interfaces. Patients book appointments and ambulances and read their own records; doctors manage schedules, prescriptions, and medical history; admins oversee doctors, ambulances, and reports. The blood bank is a self-contained module with its own donor registry, stock view, and request queue.
architecture: Every page includes a session guard before it emits any output, so authorisation is decided before a query runs rather than after. A shared Security class centralises the primitives — password_hash at cost 12, random_bytes tokens, htmlspecialchars with ENT_QUOTES for output, filter_var for email — so no page invents its own escaping.

architectureDiagram.caption: IHMS resolves the session guard before any page emits output, so authorisation happens before a query runs.

features.title: Three role-separated dashboards
features.description: Patient, doctor, and admin each get their own directory of pages and their own permitted actions, checked per request.

features.title: Blood bank module
features.description: Donor registry with add, edit, and delete, searchable by blood group, plus a stock view and a request queue for matching donors to needs.

features.title: Ambulance dispatch
features.description: Patients submit booking requests and track their own; admins manage the fleet and assign vehicles.

features.title: Clinical records
features.description: Appointments, prescriptions, medical history, health logs, and downloadable reports, each scoped to the patient they belong to.

features.title: Reproducible schema
features.description: db_migrate.php and db_seed_demo.php rebuild the database and populate demo data, so a fresh checkout reaches a working state without manual SQL.

challenges.challenge: Without a framework, an unguarded page is a complete authorisation bypass — the URL is the only thing standing between a patient and another patient's records.
challenges.learned: Made the session guard the first include on every page, before any output. Doing the check after rendering has begun is too late to redirect, and that ordering constraint is exactly what a framework's middleware normally enforces for you.

challenges.challenge: Escaping applied ad hoc at each output site gets missed somewhere, and one miss is an XSS hole.
challenges.learned: Centralised it in a Security class with htmlspecialchars(ENT_QUOTES, UTF-8) and recursive array handling, so nested form input is covered by the same call. Consistency matters more than cleverness here — the risk is the site you forget, not the one you write carefully.

challenges.challenge: Six modules touching one schema drift apart quickly when the database is set up by hand.
challenges.learned: Added migration and seed scripts so the schema has a single source of truth in the repository. Being able to reset to a known state turns schema bugs into reproducible ones.

results.description: Appointments, prescriptions, records, ambulance, blood bank, chatbot
Patient, doctor, and admin with separate page trees
password_hash with bcrypt work factor 12, never plaintext or MD5

title: UIU CGPA Calculator
description: A lightweight student utility for credit-weighted GPA and CGPA calculations, retake scenarios, and assessment tracking.
impact: A lightweight student utility for credit-weighted GPA and CGPA calculations, retake scenarios, and assessment tracking.
overview: A client-side academic planning utility for UIU students, combining a CGPA calculator, assessment tracker, and grading-policy reference in one interface.
problem: Students need to understand how course credits, expected grades, and retakes affect their trimester GPA and overall CGPA without rebuilding the same spreadsheet each time.
solution: Provide focused calculator, assessment, and policy views. Let students enter course information and inspect credit-weighted results and projected grade scenarios directly in the browser.
architecture: A React and TypeScript single-page app built with Vite. Form components calculate and pass typed GPA results and chart data to the result display; assessment tracking and grading-policy views are separate components. The core calculator does not require a server or an account.

features.description: Calculate trimester GPA and overall CGPA from course credits and grades.

features.title: Retakes and grade scenarios
features.description: Explore how retaken courses and expected grades change the calculation.

features.title: Assessment tracking
features.description: Review course assessment inputs alongside a dedicated grading-policy reference.

title: UIU Cover Page Generator
description: A browser-based utility for creating assignment cover pages, exporting A4 PDFs, and merging a cover with an existing assignment.
impact: A browser-based utility for creating assignment cover pages, exporting A4 PDFs, and merging a cover with an existing assignment.
overview: A small document-preparation tool that turns student and course details into an assignment cover page, with preview, PDF export, and optional assignment-file merging.
problem: Preparing a consistent cover page and attaching it to an assignment is repetitive, especially when the final submission needs to be a single PDF.
solution: Collect the cover information in a form, render a preview, and export an A4 cover PDF. Optionally prepend it to an uploaded assignment PDF so the student can download one submission file.
architecture: React and TypeScript manage the form and preview. html2canvas renders the cover at a fixed A4 layout, jsPDF creates the cover PDF, and pdf-lib combines it with assignment pages in the browser. Mammoth supports a Word-import conversion path, whose layout fidelity depends on the document.

features.title: Cover preview
features.description: Populate student and course information and preview the assignment cover before export.

features.title: A4 PDF export
features.description: Generate an A4 cover with a course- and student-based filename.

features.title: One submission file
features.description: Merge the generated cover with an assignment PDF, with progress feedback during preparation.
